newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. looks for decisions from Yeltsin at summit.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. looks for decisions from Yeltsin at summit.

text.p: After months of paralysis in Russian politics caused by President Boris Yeltsin's illness, U.S. officials are hoping a recuperated Yeltsin will make key decisions at a Helsinki summit this month.
The vexed issue of NATO expansion tops the agenda at the March 20-21 meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton but Washington wants to push forward also on arms control and economic reform in Russia.

The two leaders last met in Moscow in April but relations have stagnated since then as a result of Russia's presidential elections in June and July followed by Yeltsin's bouts with heart disease and pneumonia.
"I think there's been drift in Russian policymaking over the last year -- you have not seen substantial movement on any issue which requires tough decisions," a senior U.S. official said.
In recent weeks Yeltsin, who had heart bypass surgery in November and pneumonia this year, has been making a comeback and seeking to reassert his control over the Kremlin.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who met him in Moscow on Feb. 21, said he was "very much in charge," and Yeltsin vowed in a state of the union speech on Thursday to restore order in Russia and make sweeping changes.
MAJOR TEST OF YELTSIN RECOVERY

This month's summit was originally supposed to be in the United States but was moved to Helsinki in deference to Yeltsin's health problems. It will be a major test of his recovery under the glare of foreign television cameras.

The main aim of U.S. leaders is to move toward some sort of accommodation with Yeltsin on the issue of NATO expansion, which will come to a head at a NATO summit in July that will invite membership applications from East European countries.

Moscow has been unremittingly hostile to the idea of its former Warsaw Pact partners joining the Western alliance and Yeltsin attacked the plan again on Thursday, calling it an attempt to "squeeze" Russia out of Europe.

No one is expecting Yeltsin to change his mind in Helsinki -- "we would be astonished" if he did, one U.S. official said. But Washington is seeking progress on a sweetener for Moscow -- a charter or other document that would define Russia-NATO ties and ensure a permanent mechanism such as a joint council for regular dialogue and cooperation.
U.S. officials have resisted Russian pressure for a legally binding document that would give some say to the Kremlin on future development of NATO.

The alliance hopes the charter will be complete by the time of its summit in Madrid, but one U.S. official said: "We're not necessarily expecting it to be done by Madrid. This is a long, difficult process."
CONCESSIONS ON ARMS CONTROL

In addition, NATO is offering Moscow arms control concessions in the form of amendments to the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty that would ban the alliance from piling up weapons on Russia's borders. In return, the United States would like to see progress toward Russian ratification of the 1993 START-2 strategic arms treaty, which cuts the two countries' nuclear arsenals by some two-thirds.

Both governments are interested in a new START-3 round of negotiations on further cuts, but the earlier pact must be ratified first. U.S. officials concede that opposition to the treaty in the Russian Duma (parliament) is as strong as ever.

Another U.S. priority is agreement on defence systems against short-range ballistic missiles. The two countries were to have signed a first-stage deal on this last October but Russia stalled, demanding more progress on the second stage.

On the economic front, the United States is willing to promote Russian entry into key forums like the World Trade Organisation, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development and the Paris Club, which discusses rescheduling of government-to-government debt.
Washington's price, however, is that Russia should "do the necessary," as one official put it, on domestic economic reforms that the United States feels have not gone far enough.

Clinton and his aides are expected to raise once again in Helsinki their concerns over Russian sales of conventional arms and nuclear generating equipment to Iran, considered a pariah state by Washington.
Previous discussions with Russian leaders have failed to satisfy the United States on this score.
